segments.caption: A smoke alarm can be wrong in two ways.
It rings when there's no fire, or it stays silent during a real one.
Statistical tests make the same two mistakes.
Here's the definition, in simple words.
A Type 1 error is a false alarm: rejecting the null when it was actually true.
A Type 2 error is a miss: keeping the null when it was actually false.
Picture all four outcomes.
The null is either true or false, and you either reject it or keep it.
Two boxes are correct. The other two are the errors.
Think of a medical test.
Telling a healthy person they're sick? Type 1: a false alarm.
Telling a sick person they're healthy? Type 2: a miss.
The chance of a Type 1 error is called alpha, usually 5%.
So when nothing's going on, about 1 test in 20 still raises a false alarm.
The chance of a Type 2 error is beta, and 1 minus beta is called power.
Here's the catch: the two errors trade off.
Make the test stricter, and you get fewer false alarms, but more misses.
The way to reduce both? Collect more data.
So which mistake is worse? It depends.
Missing a disease can be deadly, so screening tests avoid Type 2 errors.
Jailing an innocent person is a Type 1 error, so courts demand strong evidence.
So remember: Type 1 is a false alarm. Type 2 is a miss.
Stricter tests trade one for the other, and more data helps with both.
Quick quiz!
A spam filter sends a real email from your boss to the spam folder.
Which type of error is that?
Type 1!
The null says the email is normal, and the filter wrongly rejected it. A false alarm.
